newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right takes lead in key city poll.
newsitem.headline: French far-right takes lead in key city poll.

text.p: Voters in Dreux, central France, gave the far-right National Front a first-round victory over the governing centre-right on Sunday in a key municipal poll that had been portrayed as a referendum on government policies.

A National Front slate led by European parliamentarian Marie-France Stirbois led with 36 percent of the vote and will face a combined centre-right slate led by incumbent mayor Gerard Hamel in a run-off next Sunday.
Hamel's slate won 35 percent while a combined leftist slate finished third with 25 percent. Minor parties took the rest.

Should the National Front win the run-off, Dreux would become only the fourth municipality in France where Jean-Marie Le Pen's party runs city hall. The others, won by the Front last year, are the southern cities of Toulon, Orange and Marignane.

Dreux, a town of 35,000 people about 80 km (50 miles) west of Paris, is best known in France as the scene of one of the first electoral breakthroughs by the virulently anti-immigration National Front.
The Front scored so well in a 1983 city poll that local officials of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR), the senior partner in the current governing coalition, offered it an alliance.
The resulting electoral pact scandalised the left and was also denounced by national party leaders including now-president Jacques Chirac.

But it left the right in Dreux so strong that the opposition Socialists have been excluded from local power for a generation, failing even to qualify for a run-off in the last 23 years of municipal voting.

With the national government plumbing new lows in approval ratings and unemployment at a record 12.6 percent, both the left and the far-right had urged Dreux voters to make the election a referendum on the national government.

Hamel -- whose 1995 election victory was invalidated by the the state council, France's highest constitutional authority, due to a conflict of interest -- had sought to frame the vote as a referendum on his unfinished agenda.
The National Front slate finished ahead of Hamel's in the 1995 poll as well. But Hamel defeated Stirbois in the run-off, by 61 percent to 39 percent.
Following Sunday's vote, the RPR said in a statement that Hamel had done better in this year's poll than in the first round of 1995 voting and predicted he would win the run-off.
But Dreux has been hard hit by unemployment and has a large immigrant population -- factors that the Front has used to its advantage in other recent polls.
With voters increasingly concerned by soaring urban crime and unemployment, the far-right party has been winning higher scores in by-elections and climbing in public opinion surveys across France.

The party's ratings rose even after Le Pen, who won 15 percent in last year's presidential election, said recently that he believed in racial inequality, triggering a storm of protest from mainstream politicians.
